1.title: Identity and Access Management
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Identity and Access Management. This module covers the second domain of the exam, Security and Compliance, and task statement two point three. You will learn who can do what in an A W S account, and how each person or program proves who it is. It is one of the most heavily tested topics in the whole domain.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Explain why the root user needs special care, and name the tasks only it can do. Tell I A M users, groups and roles apart, and say when each one fits. Read the parts of an I A M policy and apply least privilege. Choose among passwords, access keys, multi-factor authentication, and temporary credentials. And match Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, I A M Identity Center, Amazon Cognito and Directory Service to the need.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's First AWS Account
1.text: Meet Tidewater Outfitters, a fictional online shop for outdoor gear. It has just opened its first A W S account, using the founder's email address. Five staff need the console, and a contractor must read one bucket of product photos. The web servers read product images from storage, and one developer keeps keys in a shared file. Soon customers will sign in to a mobile app and upload photos of their gear. Your job is to give each of them the right access, and nothing more.

1.title: Authentication and Authorization: Two Questions
1.text: Access control starts with two different questions. Authentication asks, who are you? A password, a code from a device, or a key proves it. Authorization asks, what may you do? Permissions written in policies decide that. A principal is any identity that can send a request: the root user, an I A M user, or an I A M role. A W S Identity and Access Management, called I A M, controls both, and it adds no charge of its own. One more detail: I A M changes are eventually consistent, so a new user or policy can take a moment to take effect. Exam tip: who is signing in is authentication; what is allowed is authorization.

1.title: The Root User: All Power, Few Uses
1.text: Every A W S account begins with a single sign-in identity, the root user. It has complete access to every service and resource in the account. You sign in with the email address and password that were used to create the account. Notice two limits on what you can do about it. You cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user, and you cannot set a permissions boundary for it. In an A W S Organizations member account, service control policies still apply to it. The rule is simple: use the root user only for the few tasks that need it. Exam tip: the root user is not an I A M user, and everyday work should never be done with it.

1.title: Protecting the Root User: Habits That Matter
1.text: Five habits protect the root user. First, turn on multi-factor authentication. A W S requires it for every root user, so register a device at first sign-in or within the fourteen-day grace period. Second, use a strong, unique password, kept in a password manager. Third, do not create access keys for the root user, and delete any that exist. Fourth, use a group email address that several people watch, not one person's inbox, so a message from A W S is never stuck with someone on holiday. Fifth, create an administrative identity for daily work. In A W S Organizations, you can also remove root credentials from member accounts. Exam tip: think M F A, no access keys, and no daily use.

1.title: Tasks Only the Root User Can Do
1.text: A short list of tasks needs root credentials. About the account itself: changing a standalone account's settings, such as its email address, closing or reopening it, and restoring permissions after an administrator lock-out. In billing: activating I A M access to the Billing and Cost Management console, plus some billing tasks and tax invoices. For storage and queues: enabling M F A delete on an S three bucket, and fixing a policy that locks everyone out. And a few others: registering as a Reserved Instance Marketplace seller, signing up for A W S GovCloud, and recovering a key that K M S can no longer manage. Older study lists also name changing the Support plan; the current page does not. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, check the I A M page for the live list. Exam tip: account-level tasks and lock-outs need the root user; creating users or launching instances does not.

1.title: IAM Users, Groups and Roles
1.text: Three identity building blocks come up again and again. An I A M user is an identity with long-term credentials: a password, and up to two access keys. An I A M group is a set of users that share permissions. A group is not something that signs in. An I A M role has no long-term credentials at all. Whoever assumes the role receives temporary credentials for that session. Use I A M users only where federation or roles cannot be used, such as certain third-party tools. Exam tip: long-term credentials mean a user; temporary credentials mean a role.

1.title: IAM Groups: One Place for Shared Permissions
1.text: Groups make permissions easier to manage. Attach an identity-based policy to a group, and every user in it receives those permissions. A group can hold many users, and one user can belong to several groups. Groups cannot be nested: they contain users only, never other groups. There is no default group that contains every user, so you create one and add users yourself. A group also cannot be a principal in a policy, because it carries permissions, not a sign-in identity. A practical tip for Tidewater: when someone changes jobs, move them between groups instead of editing their permissions. Exam tip: groups simplify permissions for users; they do not sign in and cannot contain groups.

1.title: IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials
1.text: A role is an identity with permissions that is meant to be assumed by anyone or anything that needs it. Assuming a role returns temporary security credentials for that session. Who can assume one? I A M users, other roles, A W S services such as Amazon E C two and Lambda, and federated people. Look at the picture. An E C two instance has a role attached. A W S delivers that role's temporary credentials to the instance, and the instance reads the S three bucket. No keys are stored anywhere. Some services also create service-linked roles, tied to that service, which assumes them for you. Exam tip: for an application running on A W S that needs access, the answer is a role, not stored keys.

1.title: Cross-Account Access and Federation
1.text: Roles are also how access crosses account boundaries. A role in your account can be assumed by a user in another account. Two policies work together. The trust policy says who may assume the role. The permissions policy says what they may do once they have. Federation works in a similar way. People use an identity from an outside provider, using S A M L two point zero, which is the Security Assertion Markup Language, or Open I D Connect, and they receive a role with temporary credentials. A W S recommends federation for human users, so people do not need long-term I A M users. Exam tip: cross-account access and federation both end the same way, with a role and temporary credentials.

1.title: Reading an IAM Policy
1.text: A policy is a document, usually written in J S O N, made of one or more statements. Each statement has an Effect, which is Allow or Deny. It names the Actions, which say what can be done, such as reading an object. It names the Resources, which say what it can be done to, such as one bucket. And it may have a Condition, which says when it applies, for example only with M F A, or only over T L S. A resource-based policy also names a Principal, who is allowed. An identity-based policy does not, because the principal is the identity it is attached to. One rule to remember: an explicit Deny always wins over an Allow. Exam tip: you do not need to write J S O N, but you do need to know what these parts do.

1.title: Policy Types: Identity-Based and Resource-Based
1.text: Two policy types do the granting. Identity-based policies attach to a user, a group or a role. They come in three kinds: A W S managed policies, which A W S creates; customer managed policies, which you create; and inline policies, which belong to one identity only. Resource-based policies attach to a resource and name the principal. Examples are an Amazon S three bucket policy and a role's trust policy. A W S managed policies are a good start, but they are written for everyone, so they may grant more than you need. Customer managed policies give precise control and can be reused. Exam tip: a policy on a bucket that names who may read it is resource-based.

1.title: Guardrails Limit; Policies Grant
1.text: This slide goes beyond the exam guide, but it explains a common trap. A permissions boundary sets the maximum that an identity-based policy can give to one user or role. A service control policy in A W S Organizations sets the maximum for whole accounts, including each account's root user. Neither one grants anything. An identity policy or a resource policy must still allow the action. And when policies conflict, an explicit Deny in any of them overrides every Allow. For Tidewater, think of guardrails as the fence, and policies as the gates inside it. Exam tip: if a policy limits or caps permissions, it is a boundary or a service control policy, not a grant.

1.title: Least Privilege in Practice
1.text: Least privilege means giving only the permissions a task needs, on the resources it needs, under the conditions that fit. In practice, you may start with an A W S managed policy, then narrow it with a customer managed policy. I A M Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the activity recorded in A W S CloudTrail. Last accessed information shows permissions that are never used, so you can remove them. Review and remove unused users, roles, permissions and credentials on a regular schedule. And add conditions, for example to require M F A or T L S. Exam tip: when two answers both work, choose the one that grants fewer permissions.

1.title: Passwords and Access Keys
1.text: Now the credentials themselves. The default password policy requires between eight and one hundred twenty-eight characters, three of the four character types, and no match with the account name or email address. Passwords never expire by default. A custom policy can set a minimum length from six to one hundred twenty-eight, an expiry from one to one thousand ninety-five days, and prevent reuse of one to twenty-four passwords. The policy does not cover the root user or access keys, and there is no lockout setting. Access keys are an I D plus a secret, a user can have two, and the secret is shown only when you create the key. Never put keys in code, and never create them for the root user. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, these values come from the I A M User Guide. Exam tip: prefer roles to keys.

2.title: Multi-Factor Authentication
2.text: Multi-factor authentication adds a second factor to the sign-in: something you have, in addition to the password. A W S supports three types. Passkeys and security keys use public key cryptography and resist phishing, so A W S recommends them first. Virtual authenticator apps on a phone generate time-based one-time passwords. Hardware tokens show a six-digit code. S M S text message M F A is no longer supported. The root user and each I A M user can register up to eight M F A devices, and one is enough to sign in. As of the fourth of November, twenty twenty-six, the supported types are listed in the I A M User Guide. Exam tip: M F A is something you know plus something you have, and passkeys and security keys resist phishing best.

2.title: Where to Keep Secrets: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store
2.text: Applications need secrets, and they should never sit in the code. A W S Secrets Manager stores and retrieves secrets such as database credentials, A P I keys and tokens, and it can rotate them automatically. The application fetches the secret at run time, so no hard-coded credentials are needed. Secrets are encrypted with K M S, and access is controlled with I A M. A W S Systems Manager Parameter Store is for configuration values, such as endpoints and approved image identifiers. Its SecureString type encrypts a value with K M S. But Parameter Store does not rotate credentials, and A W S points to Secrets Manager for passwords and keys. Exam tip: credentials that must rotate, Secrets Manager; plain settings, Parameter Store.

2.title: IAM Identity Center: One Front Door for Your Workforce
2.text: I A M Identity Center gives your workforce single sign-on to many A W S accounts and to A W S applications. You can manage people in its own directory, or connect an existing identity provider. A permission set is a template of policies. When you assign one, Identity Center creates roles in each target account. Users reach everything through the A W S access portal, with M F A available. Best practice is an organization instance, in the A W S Organizations management account. A note on names: this service was called A W S Single Sign-On before it was renamed, and older material still uses that name. Exam tip: for workforce single sign-on across many accounts, choose I A M Identity Center.

2.title: Amazon Cognito and AWS Directory Service
2.text: Two services solve different directory problems. Amazon Cognito is for your application's customers. A user pool is a user directory that signs people in and issues tokens, including through Google or Apple. An identity pool swaps a trusted sign-in for temporary A W S credentials, so the app can reach services like S three. Look at the picture: the mobile app signs in through the user pool, then receives credentials from the identity pool. A W S Directory Service is for Microsoft Active Directory. A W S Managed Microsoft A D is a real directory running in A W S. A D Connector passes sign-ins through to your on-premises directory. Simple A D is a small, compatible directory. Exam tip: customers of your app, Cognito; Windows and Active Directory needs, Directory Service.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Identity and Access
2.text: Here are the look-alike pairs this task statement likes. User or role: long-term credentials, or temporary ones. Group or role: shared permissions for users, or an identity you assume. Identity-based or resource-based: attached to who, or attached to what. Limit or grant: guardrails cap, policies allow. Secrets Manager or Parameter Store: rotating credentials, or plain configuration. Identity Center or Cognito: your workforce, or your app's customers. And Managed A D, A D Connector or Simple A D: a real directory, a pass-through, or a small one. Exam tip: name the need first, then the service.

2.title: Design Check: Tidewater's Access Plan
2.text: Time to design. Look at Tidewater's six needs, and answer each one yourself before I do. The founder's sign-in is the root user, with M F A, locked away and used only for root-only tasks. The five staff get I A M Identity Center users and permission sets, not shared logins. The contractor gets a role, or a permission set, that allows read on that one bucket only, for a limited time. The web servers get a role for the E C two instances, with no keys. The developer's shared key file is deleted, and replaced by a role, or by Secrets Manager for a credential that must exist. And the mobile app customers use a Cognito user pool plus an identity pool.

2.title: Try It: Least Privilege in Twenty Minutes (Optional)
2.text: This one is optional, and the exam does not test hands-on work. If you want to try it, use a practice account. I A M costs nothing. Sign in as an administrator, not as the root user. Create a group called ReadOnlyPhotos, and attach a customer managed policy that allows only reading objects in one test bucket. Add a test user to the group, sign in as that user, and read an object. Then try to delete one, and watch it fail. Open the Access Advisor tab to see what was used. When you are done, delete the test user, group, policy and bucket. The command on screen lists the policies attached to the group. Exam tip: hands-on work is not tested on this exam, but it helps the ideas stay in your head.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. The root user has complete access: use M F A, create no access keys, and never use it day to day. Users have long-term credentials, groups share permissions, and roles give temporary credentials. Identity-based and resource-based policies grant; boundaries and service control policies only limit; and an explicit deny wins. For least privilege, start small, use Access Analyzer and last accessed information, and add conditions. For credentials, know the password policy, two access keys per user, and M F A with passkeys, apps or hardware tokens, and no S M S. And for services: Secrets Manager for secrets, Parameter Store for settings, Identity Center for the workforce, Cognito for app customers, and Directory Service for Active Directory.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which A W S identity is created with the account, has complete access to everything in it, and should be used only for the few tasks that require it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, the A W S account root user. It signs in with the email address and password used at sign-up. An I A M user, a role or an Identity Center administrator is created later and can be limited.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which task requires you to sign in as the root user? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Restoring permissions when the only I A M administrator has locked themselves out needs root credentials. Creating groups, attaching policies and launching instances are everyday tasks that an administrative identity can perform.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. This one asks you to select two. Tidewater's founder signed up with a personal email address. Which two actions best protect the root user? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. M F A protects the sign-in, and an administrative identity keeps the root user out of daily use. Root access keys, daily use of the root user, and sharing its password all widen the exposure of the most powerful identity in the account.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Tidewater's web servers on Amazon E C two must read product photos from an Amazon S three bucket. What is the best way to grant that access? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A role delivers temporary credentials to the instances automatically, so no long-term keys are stored. Keys in a file can leak, root keys give far too much power, and a public policy would expose the photos to everyone.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A policy attached to an Amazon S three bucket that names which principals may read its objects is an example of which policy type? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, a resource-based policy. A policy attached to a resource that names the principals allowed to use it is resource-based. Boundaries and service control policies only limit permissions, and an identity-based policy is attached to a user, group or role.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A developer must read objects in one S three bucket and nothing else. Which approach best follows the principle of least privilege? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A narrow customer managed policy grants only the actions the task needs on only the resource it needs. Administrator access, full S three access, and shared administrator credentials all give far more than the task requires.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two are M F A options that A W S supports for I A M users? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D: a passkey or security key, and a virtual authenticator app. A W S also supports hardware tokens. A W S has ended support for enabling S M S text message M F A, and security questions and email codes are not M F A options for I A M.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Tidewater's mobile app lets customers sign up with an email address or a Google account, and then upload photos to Amazon S three with limited permissions. Which combination meets this need? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A Cognito user pool signs customers in, including through Google, and an identity pool exchanges that sign-in for temporary, limited A W S credentials. Per-customer I A M users with stored keys do not scale, Identity Center is for your workforce, and Directory Service is for Active Directory needs.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: C. Question two: D. Question three: B and E. Question four: A. Question five: C. Question six: B. Question seven: A and D. Question eight: D. That completes Module four. Next, Module five covers the security services that protect an account: firewalls, threat detection, vulnerability scanning and encryption keys.
